# 1-Week Deload Protocol
### Client Profile: Advanced Male, 26 | Post-High-Volume Hypertrophy Block | Week 5 of 12

---

## Programming Philosophy for This Deload

After four weeks of sustained high-volume work at RPE 8.5, your client's central and peripheral fatigue will be meaningfully accumulated even if subjective soreness has plateaued — a classic sign that the body has adapted to the stress rather than recovered from it. The goal of this week is **not** to maintain fitness; it is to dissipate fatigue so that the subsequent intensification block can be attacked from a fully recovered baseline. Fitness will be temporarily suppressed this week, but it will supercompensate once fatigue clears, which is precisely the mechanism the next phase will exploit.

The deload follows two simple rules: **same exercises, reduced volume, reduced intensity.** Keeping the movement patterns identical preserves motor skill and avoids any neural novelty that could itself generate fatigue. Volume drops to approximately **40–50% of working sets** (roughly 8–9 working sets per session rather than 18), and intensity drops to **RPE 5–6**, which corresponds to leaving 4–5 reps in reserve on every set. There is no grinding, no chasing pumps, and no heroic effort. If a set feels easy, that is correct.

---

## Session Structure Overview

Assuming the client trained on a **4-day upper/lower or push/pull/legs variant** during the hypertrophy block, the deload mirrors that split across four sessions with one additional optional active recovery day. If the client ran a different split, the set/rep prescriptions below translate directly — simply map them onto whatever session structure was used.

| Day | Session | Working Sets | Target RPE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monday | Session A (e.g. Upper / Push) | 8–9 | 5–6 |
| Tuesday | Session B (e.g. Lower / Pull) | 8–9 | 5–6 |
| Wednesday | Active Recovery / Off | — | — |
| Thursday | Session C (e.g. Upper / Push repeat) | 8–9 | 5–6 |
| Friday | Session D (e.g. Lower / Pull repeat) | 8–9 | 5–6 |
| Saturday | Optional light movement | — | — |
| Sunday | Full rest | — | — |

---

## Session-by-Session Detail

### Session A — Upper Push (Monday)

The session opens with the same compound movements your client has been performing, but the loading and volume are deliberately conservative. Begin with a thorough warm-up — two to three progressively loaded warm-up sets per compound, none of which count toward working sets. This warm-up structure should actually feel more substantial relative to the working sets than usual, which is intentional.

**Barbell Bench Press**
3 sets × 6 reps at RPE 5–6. Select a load that represents roughly 65–70% of the weight used in week 4. The bar should move fast and feel almost trivially light. Rest 2 minutes between sets. The purpose here is groove, not stimulus.

**Overhead Press (Barbell or Dumbbell — whichever was used in the hypertrophy block)**
3 sets × 6 reps at RPE 5–6. Same loading logic — approximately 65% of recent working weight. Focus on clean technique and full range of motion without any compensatory lean or tempo manipulation to make it harder.

**Incline Dumbbell Press**
2 sets × 8 reps at RPE 5. This is a single-joint accessory in the context of the deload. Keep the load light, the movement smooth, and resist any temptation to add a drop set or extend the set.

**Lateral Raises**
1 set × 12 reps, light. This is purely movement maintenance. One set is sufficient.

Total working sets: **9**. Session duration should be noticeably shorter than the hypertrophy weeks — approximately 45 minutes including warm-up. If the client finishes and feels like they could do more, that is the correct outcome.

---

### Session B — Lower / Pull (Tuesday)

**Barbell Back Squat (or whichever primary lower compound was used)**
3 sets × 5 reps at RPE 5–6. Load at approximately 65% of week 4 working weight. Five reps rather than six keeps total volume slightly lower on the most systemically taxing movement in the programme. Rest 2–3 minutes. Cue the client to focus on positional quality — bracing, depth, bar path — rather than output.

**Romanian Deadlift**
3 sets × 6 reps at RPE 5. This is a posterior chain maintenance movement. The load should feel almost conversational. Emphasise the hip hinge and hamstring stretch rather than loading.

**Barbell or Dumbbell Row (whichever was used in the hypertrophy block)**
3 sets × 6 reps at RPE 5–6. Approximately 65% of recent working weight. Full range of motion, controlled eccentric, no momentum.

Total working sets: **9**. Again, the session should feel incomplete by the standards of the last four weeks. Reassure the client that this is the adaptation mechanism working as intended.

---

### Wednesday — Active Recovery

This day is not a training day. However, complete rest is not mandatory and for many advanced clients can feel psychologically uncomfortable. Appropriate options include a 20–30 minute walk at a conversational pace, light mobility work targeting whatever areas accumulated the most tightness during the hypertrophy block (commonly the thoracic spine, hip flexors, and lats), or a single round of foam rolling and static stretching. Nothing that elevates heart rate meaningfully, nothing that creates muscular fatigue. If the client genuinely feels fatigued, full rest is the better choice.

---

### Session C — Upper Push Repeat (Thursday)

This session mirrors Session A with identical exercises. The loading can remain the same as Monday or drop fractionally if the client reports any residual fatigue. There is no progression within the deload week — do not add weight, do not add reps, do not add sets.

**Barbell Bench Press** — 3 × 6 at RPE 5–6
**Overhead Press** — 3 × 6 at RPE 5–6
**Incline Dumbbell Press** — 2 × 8 at RPE 5
**Lateral Raises** — 1 × 12, light

Total working sets: **9**

---

### Session D — Lower / Pull Repeat (Friday)

This session mirrors Session B.

**Barbell Back Squat** — 3 × 5 at RPE 5–6
**Romanian Deadlift** — 3 × 6 at RPE 5
**Barbell or Dumbbell Row** — 3 × 6 at RPE 5–6

Total working sets: **9**

---

## Nutrition During the Deload

Because training volume and intensity are both reduced, total energy expenditure will drop modestly. The recommendation is to **maintain caloric intake at the same level as the hypertrophy block** rather than cutting calories. The client's body is in a repair and consolidation phase, and adequate energy availability supports that process. Protein should remain at the same absolute intake — a minimum of 1.8–2.2g per kilogram of bodyweight — to continue supporting muscle protein synthesis and tissue repair. There is no need to carbohydrate cycle or reduce carbohydrates; glycogen replenishment supports recovery. If the client is in a caloric surplus, maintain it. If in a deficit, consider bringing calories to maintenance for this single week to maximise the recovery effect before the intensification block begins.

---

## Sleep and Recovery Emphasis

This is the week to be deliberate about sleep. Encourage the client to target a minimum of 8 hours per night, prioritising consistent sleep and wake times. Growth hormone secretion during slow-wave sleep is a primary driver of the tissue repair that makes the deload productive. If the client uses any recovery modalities — contrast showers, sauna, massage — this is an appropriate week to use them, though none are mandatory. Alcohol should be minimised, as it directly impairs sleep architecture and protein synthesis.

---

## Psychological Coaching Note for the Trainer

Advanced clients frequently resist deloads because the subjective experience of reduced effort conflicts with their training identity. It is worth explicitly framing this week as **a performance tool, not a rest week in the colloquial sense.** The client is not taking time off; they are executing a specific physiological protocol designed to maximise the output of the intensification block that follows. The measure of a successful deload is not how hard the sessions felt — it is how the client performs in Week 6. If they enter the intensification block feeling fresh, motivated, and slightly hungry to train, the deload has done its job precisely.

---

*Ready to build the intensification block for Weeks 6–12 whenever you are.*

## Clarifying the Volume Baseline

I don't have the specific exercise selection or session structure from your client's hypertrophy block — I generated the deload using the **18 working sets per session** figure you provided, but I made assumptions about the split and exercise choices to populate the sessions.

To give you precise per-session deload targets anchored to his actual last week, I need a couple of things from you:

---

**1. What was his training split?**
For example: upper/lower, push/pull/legs, full body, or a custom arrangement.

**2. How many sessions did he run per week?**
18 sets per session across how many days — 4, 5, 6?

**3. What were the actual exercises per session?**
Even a rough list per day is enough. For example: *Day 1 — squat, RDL, leg press, leg curl, calf raise.*

**4. Were all sessions at 18 sets, or did volume vary by day?**
Some programmes run higher volume on priority days and slightly lower on secondary days. If his sessions weren't uniform, the per-session deload targets should reflect that asymmetry rather than applying a flat percentage across the board.

---

Once you give me those details I'll calculate the exact working set targets per session, map them to his specific exercises, and give you a clean numbers table you can take straight into the deload week.

## Bench Press Substitution — Cranky Shoulder

Before I recommend a swap, a few quick questions that will determine the right choice:

---

**1. Where specifically is the discomfort?**
For example: anterior deltoid, AC joint, pec minor insertion, or general front-of-shoulder. The location changes the recommendation meaningfully.

- **AC joint irritation** typically means wide grip and deep ROM are the problem — a closer grip or floor press may be sufficient
- **Anterior deltoid / bicep tendon** irritation often means horizontal pressing with the arm in front of the body is the issue — an incline or neutral grip variation may offload it
- **Pec minor / coracoid area** often responds well to reducing the degree of shoulder extension at the bottom of the press

**2. Is it the range of motion, the load, or the position that aggravates it?**
Does it hurt at the bottom of the press, throughout, or only under heavy load? That tells us whether it's a stretch-position problem, a compression problem, or purely load-dependent.

**3. Has he seen a physio or is this self-reported crankiness?**
If it's been assessed, I'll work within whatever restrictions were given. If it's unassessed, I'll err on the conservative side and flag it.

---

Even a rough answer to question 1 gets us most of the way there. If you're not sure, tell me what he's told you and we'll work from that.

## Adding a Mobility Session

I can build a 20-minute mobility session and slot it into the week. A couple of quick questions to make sure it's targeted and useful rather than generic:

---

**1. Are there any known restrictions or priority areas?**
For example: thoracic spine, hip flexors, ankle dorsiflexion, lat/shoulder complex. Given the cranky shoulder you mentioned, I'd likely include some thoracic and shoulder girdle work regardless — just want to know if there's anything else to prioritise.

**2. Where do you want it in the week?**
A few logical options given the current structure:

- **Wednesday** — already designated as the active recovery day, making it the natural home
- **As a session opener** on one of the four training days — keeps it attached to training and ensures it gets done
- **Standalone on Saturday** — gives a second lighter day between Friday's session and Sunday's full rest

**3. What's his movement background like?**
Has he done structured mobility work before or is this relatively new to him? That affects how much coaching cue detail to include in the write-up.

**4. Any equipment preferences or restrictions for the mobility work?**
Full gym is available, but some clients prefer mat-based work only for mobility sessions. Others are happy using a rack for thoracic extensions, a band for shoulder distractions, and so on.

---

Answer whichever of those you can and I'll write it up in full.

## Adding Zone 2 Cardio

I can slot two Zone 2 sessions into the week. Just a few quick questions before I place them:

---

**1. What's his preferred cardio modality?**
Given the cranky shoulder, upper body ergometers are probably off the table for now, but worth confirming. Likely options:

- **Cycling** (bike or assault bike at low effort) — joint-friendly, no spinal loading
- **Incline treadmill walk** — low impact, easy to control intensity
- **Rowing** — full body but may aggravate the shoulder depending on the issue
- **Running** — fine if he has the conditioning base, but worth confirming given he's been in a pure hypertrophy block for weeks

**2. How are we defining Zone 2 for this client?**
Options:

- **Heart rate based** — roughly 60–70% of max HR. Do you have his max HR or are we estimating from age (194 bpm estimated max for a 26-year-old, putting Zone 2 at roughly 116–136 bpm)?
- **Talk test** — conversational pace, full sentences without breathlessness
- **RPE based** — RPE 3–4, clearly aerobic, no laboured breathing

**3. Where do you want them placed?**
Do you want them on rest days to keep training days clean, or are you happy attaching them to the end of a resistance session?

---

Answer what you can and I'll integrate everything — cardio, mobility, and the updated session structure — into a clean final version of the full week.

## Strength Tracking During a Deload

This is a really important question to get right, because the instinct to test during a deload is understandable — advanced clients want data — but **true maximal testing directly contradicts the purpose of the week.** A 1RM attempt or even a heavy 3RM is a significant CNS event that would reintroduce exactly the fatigue you're trying to dissipate. So the answer isn't to avoid tracking entirely, it's to **track the right things in the right way.**

---

### The Core Principle

Rather than testing **maximal output**, track **submaximal performance indicators** — metrics that give you meaningful data about where his strength is sitting without creating a fatigue debt. The key insight is that **velocity, technique quality, and RPE at a given load** are all valid strength proxies that don't require him to push anywhere near his limit.

---

### What to Track

**1. RPE at a Fixed Submaximal Load**
This is the most practical and lowest-risk option. Select a load he used regularly during the hypertrophy block — something that was roughly RPE 7–7.5 at peak fatigue in week 4 — and note what RPE it feels like now during the deload. If the same load drops to RPE 5–6, that is direct evidence that fatigue is clearing and his underlying fitness is intact or improving. This works on every compound in his programme and requires no additional testing protocol.

Recommended loads to track this way:
- Barbell back squat
- Romanian deadlift
- Overhead press
- Primary row variation
- Bench substitute (once you've confirmed the swap)

**2. Bar Velocity on the First Working Set**
If the gym has a velocity tracker — a Gymaware, Push Band, or even a free app like Iron Path for rough estimates — log the mean concentric velocity on the first working set of each compound at a fixed load. Velocity is highly sensitive to fatigue status. As fatigue dissipates across the deload week, velocity at the same load will increase measurably even if the load itself doesn't change. This gives him a concrete, objective number to watch improve across the four sessions without ever pushing to failure.

**3. Warm-Up Set Feel at Known Loads**
A less technical but still valid method. Have him note how his standard warm-up loads feel on day one of the deload versus day four. A load that felt sticky and slow on Monday should feel crisp and fast by Friday. This is qualitative but meaningful for an advanced client who has good body awareness.

**4. Resting Heart Rate and HRV (if he tracks it)**
Not a strength marker per se, but a useful parallel data point. If he wears a fitness tracker or uses a HRV app, logging morning resting HR and HRV across the week gives you a physiological confirmation that the deload is working. Expect resting HR to drop slightly and HRV to trend upward as the week progresses. If neither moves, it may indicate the deload needs extending or that recovery outside the gym — sleep, nutrition, stress — needs attention.

**5. Movement Quality Scoring**
For an advanced client this can be surprisingly informative. Have him self-score or have you score key technical markers on the squat and hinge on day one versus day four — things like depth consistency, bar path straightness, bracing quality. Fatigue degrades movement quality in subtle ways that often go unnoticed during hard training blocks. A fresh client moves better, and documenting that shift is both motivating and useful baseline data for the intensification block.

---

### What Not to Do

Do not test a true 1RM, 3RM, or any set taken to failure this week. Do not add a heavy single "just to see where he's at." Do not extend sets beyond the prescribed RPE because the weight feels light. The feeling of strength returning mid-deload is real and it is tempting, but acting on it defeats the purpose. The time to test maximal output is **Week 6, session one** of the intensification block — that is when the data will actually mean something and when the fatigue has fully cleared.

---

### Practical Tracking Format

A simple session log works well here. For each compound, record:

| Exercise | Load Used | Reps | RPE Felt | Velocity Feel (fast / moderate / slow) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Run this across all four sessions and by Friday you'll have a clean picture of his fatigue dissipation curve — which also tells you whether he's ready to hit Week 6 hard or whether he might benefit from one additional lighter day before ramping back up.

---

Once you've confirmed the bench substitution and the cardio/mobility details, I'll integrate this tracking framework directly into the session write-ups so it's built into the programme rather than sitting separately.

## On Pushing Wednesday and Friday — A Direct Recommendation

I'd push back on this, and I want to explain exactly why rather than just saying no.

---

### What "Feeling Great by Wednesday" Actually Means

This is the deload working correctly, not a signal to increase intensity. The feeling of restored energy and motivation mid-deload is a well-documented phenomenon in advanced trainees and it is almost universally misread as readiness to train hard. What it actually represents is **partial fatigue dissipation** — the acute, surface-level fatigue from the last training sessions has cleared, but the deeper accumulated fatigue from four weeks of RPE 8.5 work has not fully resolved yet. The underlying fitness that was suppressed by that fatigue is starting to emerge, which feels like strength returning. It is not the same thing as being recovered.

If he pushes Wednesday and Friday back toward RPE 7.5–8, he will feel good during those sessions. He will then carry residual fatigue into Week 6, blunt the supercompensation effect, and underperform in exactly the intensification block this deload is designed to set up. The boredom is real. The readiness is not.

---

### The Specific Risk Here

His shoulder is already flagged as cranky. Pushing intensity on pressing variations before that tissue has had a full week of reduced load is a meaningful injury risk. Connective tissue and joint structures recover on a slower timeline than muscle — the shoulder may feel fine at RPE 6 and become aggravated again at RPE 8. A deload that ends in a shoulder flare-up going into an intensification block is a significantly worse outcome than a boring week.

---

### What You Can Do Instead

If the boredom is a genuine compliance and motivation issue — which is legitimate for advanced clients — there are ways to add engagement without adding fatigue-generating intensity.

**Option 1 — Add Technique Work**
Use the Wednesday and Friday sessions to work on a specific technical element of his compounds. Pause squats at the bottom, tempo bench press with a 3-second eccentric, or deficit deadlifts at the same light load. These add a skill and focus dimension to the session without increasing mechanical load or CNS demand. The load stays the same. The attention required goes up.

**Option 2 — Add the Velocity Tracking as a Game**
As discussed in the strength markers conversation, tracking bar speed at a fixed load gives him something to compete against. Trying to move a light bar as fast as possible is genuinely engaging for advanced clients and actually has a potentiation effect for the intensification block without generating meaningful fatigue.

**Option 3 — Slightly Increase Volume on Friday Only**
If you want to give him something, Friday is the safer place to do it than Wednesday because he has the full weekend before Week 6 begins. You could add one additional working set per compound on Friday — bringing him to 10–11 sets rather than 9 — while keeping RPE strictly at 6. This is a minor concession that gives him a slightly fuller session without meaningfully compromising the deload. I would not go beyond this.

**Option 4 — Move Week 6 Forward**
If he is genuinely recovering faster than expected — good sleep, good nutrition, low life stress — and Wednesday already feels like full recovery, it is worth considering whether he needs the full seven days. Some advanced trainees deload in 5 days rather than 7. If that's the case, you could run Wednesday and Thursday as normal deload sessions and begin Week 6 on Friday rather than the following Monday. This is a more honest response to his recovery status than pushing intensity within the deload framework.

---

### My Recommendation

Keep Wednesday at the prescribed RPE. Use one of the technique or velocity options above to address the boredom. On Friday, add one set per compound if needed as a psychological concession, but hold the RPE line at 6. Begin Week 6 on schedule.

The client feeling great is the goal. Protect that feeling so it's still there on Monday.

| Tuesday | Session B — Lower / Pull | 9 | 5–6 | ~45 min |

| Thursday | Session C — Upper Push repeat | 9 | 5–6 | ~45 min |
| Friday | Session D — Lower / Pull repeat + 1 set concession | 10–11 | 5–6 | ~50 min |
| Saturday | Zone 2 Cardio | — | HR 116–136 | 30 min |
| Sunday | Zone 2 Cardio | — | HR 116–136 | 30 min |

---

## Strength Tracking Protocol — All Four Resistance Sessions

Run this log on every compound in every resistance session. It generates a fatigue dissipation curve across the week without requiring any maximal effort and gives you clean baseline data for Week 6.

For each compound, record the following at the first working set:

| Exercise | Load Used | Reps Completed | RPE Felt | Bar Speed Feel | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**RPE felt** should be recorded honestly against the prescribed load — if a weight that was RPE 7.5 in week 4 now feels like RPE 5, note that explicitly. That delta is your primary strength marker this week.

**Bar speed feel** should be logged as fast, moderate, or slow. If the gym has a velocity tracking device, log mean concentric velocity numerically. A free app will give rough estimates if no dedicated device is available. Expect velocity at fixed loads to increase across Monday to Friday as fatigue clears. If it doesn't, sleep and nutrition need attention before Week 6 begins.

Do not chase numbers. Do not add reps because the weight feels light. Do not extend any set beyond the prescribed rep target. The tracking is observational, not competitive.

---

## Monday — Session A: Upper Push

**Warm-up:** 10 minutes. Begin with 5 minutes of light cardio to elevate core temperature — bike or treadmill at an easy pace. Follow with band pull-aparts, wall slides, and two to three progressively loaded warm-up sets on each compound. Warm-up sets do not count toward working sets.

---

**Low Incline Dumbbell Press — Neutral Grip**
*Substituting for barbell bench press due to shoulder irritation*
3 sets × 6 reps — RPE 5–6
Load at approximately 60–65% of the dumbbell or equivalent load used in week 4. The neutral grip reduces internal rotation stress on the anterior shoulder. The low incline — no more than 20–25 degrees — keeps the movement pattern close to flat pressing without the shoulder extension demand of a flat bench. The bottom position should feel comfortable and unstretched. If there is any anterior shoulder discomfort at this position, reduce the range of motion by elevating the dumbbells slightly at the bottom rather than pushing through it. Rest 2 minutes between sets.

**Overhead Press — Barbell or Dumbbell, whichever was used in the hypertrophy block**
3 sets × 6 reps — RPE 5–6
Load at approximately 65% of week 4 working weight. Bar path should be clean and vertical. No excessive lumbar extension to compensate for reduced thoracic mobility. If the shoulder reports any discomfort on the overhead pattern, switch to a landmine press for this week only, which reduces the degree of shoulder elevation and is broadly well-tolerated by irritated anterior shoulders. Rest 2 minutes.

**Cable Fly or Pec Deck — whichever is available**
2 sets × 10 reps — RPE 5
Light load, full range of motion, slow controlled eccentric. This replaces any secondary pressing accessory from the hypertrophy block and keeps mechanical stress off the shoulder while still providing a chest stimulus through the stretch-shortening cycle. Rest 90 seconds.

**Lateral Raises — Dumbbell**
1 set × 12 reps — light
Movement maintenance only. One set is sufficient. Do not add a second set because it feels easy.

**Total working sets: 9**

Session duration should be approximately 40–45 minutes including warm-up. If the client finishes and feels significantly under-stimulated, remind him that the tracking data he just collected is the productive output of the session, not the fatigue generated.

---

## Tuesday — Session B: Lower / Pull

**Warm-up:** 10 minutes. Light bike or treadmill, followed by hip circles, leg swings, and two to three progressively loaded warm-up sets on the squat.

---

**Barbell Back Squat**
3 sets × 5 reps — RPE 5–6
Load at approximately 65% of week 4 working weight. Five reps rather than six keeps total volume slightly lower on the most systemically demanding movement in the programme. Focus on positional quality — bracing, depth consistency, bar path — rather than output. The bar should move with noticeable speed. If it is grinding, the load is too high. Rest 2–3 minutes.

**Romanian Deadlift**
3 sets × 6 reps — RPE 5
Load at approximately 60–65% of week 4 working weight. Emphasise the hip hinge and hamstring stretch rather than loading. Controlled eccentric, full range of motion, no momentum at the bottom. This is a recovery movement this week, not a loading event. Rest 2 minutes.

**Barbell or Dumbbell Row — whichever was used in the hypertrophy block**
3 sets × 6 reps — RPE 5–6
Load at approximately 65% of week 4 working weight. Full range of motion, controlled eccentric, no momentum or body English. The upper back should feel engaged but not taxed. Rest 2 minutes.

**Total working sets: 9**

---

## Wednesday — Mobility Session: 20 Minutes

This is a standalone session, not a warm-up. It should be performed at a genuinely relaxed pace with full attention on quality of movement and breath. Nothing is loaded. Nothing is timed aggressively. The session targets the areas most likely to have accumulated restriction during four weeks of high-volume hypertrophy work — thoracic spine, shoulder girdle, hip flexors, and posterior chain — with additional shoulder-specific work given the flagged irritation.

Complete each drill for the prescribed duration or reps, moving through the sequence without rushing.

---

**Thoracic Spine Foam Roll**
90 seconds. Positioned across a foam roller at mid-back, arms crossed over chest. Slowly extend over the roller, pausing at any stiff segments. Move the roller incrementally up the thoracic spine. Do not roll the lumbar spine. This is the single highest-value mobility drill for someone who has been loading a barbell for four weeks.

**Cat-Cow — Quadruped**
10 slow repetitions. Full spinal flexion to full spinal extension on each rep. Breathe in on extension, out on flexion. This reintroduces segmental spinal movement that gets compressed during heavy loading weeks.

**Thread the Needle — Quadruped Thoracic Rotation**
8 repetitions each side. From a quadruped position, thread one arm under the body and rotate the thoracic spine, following the hand with the eyes. Pause at end range for 2 seconds. This directly addresses thoracic rotation restriction, which contributes to compensatory shoulder stress during pressing.

**90/90 Hip Stretch**
60 seconds each side. Seated on the floor with both legs at 90-degree angles, front and back. Sit tall, breathe into the hip. Progress to a forward fold over the front shin if comfortable. This targets hip external and internal rotation simultaneously and addresses the hip flexor and glute restriction that accumulates during heavy squat and hinge work.

**Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch with Reach**
45 seconds each side. In a half-kneeling position, posteriorly tilt the pelvis, squeeze the glute of the trailing leg, and reach the same-side arm overhead and slightly away from the body. This combines hip flexor lengthening with a lateral thoracic stretch. Given the volume of squatting and deadlifting in the hypertrophy block, hip flexor restriction is almost certain.

**Wall Slide — Shoulder Girdle**
10 repetitions. Standing with back flat against a wall, arms in a goalpost position, slide the arms overhead while maintaining contact between the back of the hands, forearms, and wall. This is directly relevant to the cranky shoulder — it trains scapular upward rotation and posterior shoulder activation in a completely unloaded environment. If the shoulder reports any discomfort during this movement, reduce the range and work only in the pain-free zone.

**Band Pull-Apart or No-Money Drill**
2 × 15 repetitions. Using a light resistance band or no band at all. Pull-aparts target the posterior shoulder and mid-traps, which are chronically under-recovered in pressing-dominant programmes. The no-money drill — starting with elbows at 90 degrees and externally rotating — specifically targets the infraspinatus and teres minor, which are relevant to anterior shoulder health.

**Doorframe or Rack Pec Stretch — Modified**
30 seconds each side. Using a rack upright rather than a doorframe for better control. Position the arm at 90 degrees of abduction — not higher — and gently lean into the stretch. Given the shoulder irritation, do not force this stretch and do not position the arm above shoulder height. A mild pull in the pec is appropriate. Any anterior shoulder pain means stopping immediately.

**Child's Pose with Lat Reach**
60 seconds. From child's pose, walk the hands to one side to bias the lat and thoracic side bend. 30 seconds each side. The lats are heavily loaded during rowing and pulling work and their restriction directly affects shoulder positioning during pressing.

**Diaphragmatic Breathing — Supine**
2 minutes. Lying on the back, knees bent, one hand on the chest and one on the belly. Breathe into the belly, allowing the diaphragm to descend. Exhale fully. This is not filler — diaphragmatic breathing directly downregulates the sympathetic nervous system and supports the recovery process. For an advanced client who has been training at high intensity for four weeks, deliberate parasympathetic activation has measurable recovery value.

**Total session time: approximately 18–22 minutes**

---

## Thursday — Session C: Upper Push Repeat

This session is identical in structure to Monday's Session A. The loading should remain the same as Monday or drop fractionally if the client reports any residual fatigue. There is no progression within the deload week. Do not add weight, do not add reps, do not add sets.

---

**Low Incline Dumbbell Press — Neutral Grip**
3 sets × 6 reps — RPE 5–6
Same load as Monday. Note RPE felt and bar speed in the tracking log and compare directly to Monday's entry. Any reduction in perceived effort at the same load is a positive data point.

**Overhead Press**
3 sets × 6 reps — RPE 5–6
Same load as Monday.

**Cable Fly or Pec Deck**
2 sets × 10 reps — RPE 5
Same load as Monday.

**Lateral Raises**
1 set × 12 reps — light

**Total working sets: 9**

---

**A note on Wednesday's energy and the boredom issue.** If the client reports feeling great by Wednesday and pushes back on the low intensity — which is likely given his training history — acknowledge it directly. The feeling of restored energy mid-deload is the deload working, not a signal to increase load. The appropriate response to feeling good on Thursday is to move the bar faster at the same load and log the velocity improvement, not to add plates. His shoulder is also still in a recovery window. Hold the line on RPE 6 through Thursday. Friday has a minor concession built in.

---

## Friday — Session D: Lower / Pull Repeat + Concession Sets

This session mirrors Tuesday's Session B with one adjustment. As a single concession to the client's motivation and the fact that he is likely well-recovered by this point in the week, one additional working set is added per compound — bringing total working sets to 11–12 rather than 9. **RPE remains strictly at 6.** This is a volume concession, not an intensity concession. The load does not increase. The effort does not increase. The session is simply slightly fuller, which addresses the psychological need without generating meaningful additional fatigue before Week 6.

---

**Barbell Back Squat**
4 sets × 5 reps — RPE 5–6
Same load as Tuesday. One additional set. Note whether RPE has dropped relative to Tuesday at the same load — this is the primary strength marker data point of the week.

**Romanian Deadlift**
4 sets × 6 reps — RPE 5
Same load as Tuesday. One additional set.

**Barbell or Dumbbell Row**
4 sets × 6 reps — RPE 5–6
Same load as Tuesday. One additional set.

**Total working sets: 12**

This is the most volume the client does in any single session this week and it is still one third of his hypertrophy block session volume. Frame it to him as the final data collection session before Week 6, not as a hard training day. By the end of this session you should have a clean four-session tracking log showing RPE and velocity trends across the week, which tells you exactly how recovered he is and how aggressively you can programme Week 6.

---

## Saturday — Zone 2 Cardio: 30 Minutes

**Modality:** Cycling or incline treadmill walk — adjust based on client preference and equipment availability. Rowing is excluded this week given the shoulder. Running is appropriate if the client has a conditioning base, but given four weeks of pure hypertrophy work, cycling or walking is the lower-risk default.

**Intensity:** Heart rate 116–136 bpm, based on estimated max HR of 194 bpm for a 26-year-old. If the client has a measured max HR, recalculate the band as 60–70% of that figure. The talk test is a reliable field check — he should be able to hold a full conversation without any breathlessness. If he cannot, the intensity is too high.

**Structure:** No warm-up or cool-down protocol required beyond the first and last few minutes of the session naturally sitting below the Zone 2 band. 30 minutes of continuous steady-state work. No intervals, no surges, no pushing the upper end of the HR band. This is aerobic system maintenance, not a cardiovascular training stimulus.

**Purpose:** Four weeks of high-volume hypertrophy work with no dedicated aerobic work will have modestly reduced mitochondrial density and cardiac output efficiency. Two Zone 2 sessions this week maintain the aerobic base without generating any fatigue that competes with the recovery process. Zone 2 work at this intensity also actively supports recovery by increasing blood flow to recovering tissues and enhancing lactate clearance.

---

## Sunday — Zone 2 Cardio: 30 Minutes

Identical protocol to Saturday. Same modality, same heart rate band, same duration. If the client is genuinely fatigued from the week — which would be unusual given the reduced training load but is possible if sleep or nutrition have been poor — replace this session with a 30-minute walk at a conversational pace, which sits at the lower boundary of Zone 2 and still delivers the blood flow and recovery benefits without any cardiovascular demand.

---

## Nutrition This Week

Maintain caloric intake at the same absolute level as the hypertrophy block. Do not reduce calories in response to the reduced training volume. The body is in an active repair and consolidation phase and requires adequate energy availability to complete that process. Reducing calories during a deload is a common mistake that blunts the recovery effect and compromises the supercompensation response going into Week 6.

Protein remains at a minimum of 1.8–2.2g per kilogram of bodyweight. Carbohydrates should be maintained — glycogen replenishment supports recovery and there is no metabolic rationale for reducing carbohydrate intake during a single-week deload. If the client is in a caloric surplus, maintain it. If in a deficit, bring calories to maintenance for this week specifically.

Hydration deserves particular attention this week. Connective tissue recovery — relevant given the shoulder — is directly supported by adequate hydration. Target a minimum of 35ml per kilogram of bodyweight per day.

---

## Sleep and Recovery

Target 8 hours per night with consistent sleep and wake times across the week. Growth hormone secretion during slow-wave sleep is a primary driver of the tissue repair that makes the deload productive. This is the week to be deliberate about sleep quality, not just duration — dark room, cool temperature, no screens in the 30 minutes before bed.

Alcohol should be minimised or eliminated this week. It directly impairs slow-wave sleep architecture and inhibits muscle protein synthesis, both of which undermine the recovery process.

If the client uses any recovery modalities — contrast showers, sauna, soft tissue work — this is an appropriate week to use them. A sports massage midweek, if accessible, would be particularly well-timed given the accumulated tissue stress from the hypertrophy block.

---

## End-of-Week Assessment

By Friday evening you should have four sessions of tracking data. Review the RPE and velocity logs and ask three questions before finalising the Week 6 programme.

First, did RPE at fixed loads drop across the week? A load that was RPE 7.5 in week 4 should feel like RPE 5–5.5 by Friday. If it does, the deload has worked and Week 6 can begin at full intensity. If it hasn't moved, consider one additional lighter day before ramping up.

Second, how is the shoulder? It should feel meaningfully better than it did at the end of week 4. If it does, the bench substitution decision for Week 6 can be revisited carefully. If it is still irritated, the neutral grip incline press stays in the programme and a physio referral is worth raising with the client.

Third, how is the client's motivation and psychological state? An advanced client who is genuinely bored and hungry to train hard by Friday is in the ideal state to begin an intensification block. That is the target outcome of this week.

---

*Ready to build the full intensification block for Weeks 6–12 when you are. Given the data this deload week will generate, Week 6 programming can be precisely calibrated to where his strength markers actually land rather than estimated from week 4 numbers.*

# Complete 1-Week Deload Protocol
### Client Profile: Advanced Male, 26 | Post-High-Volume Hypertrophy Block | Week 5 of 12

## Programming Philosophy

After four weeks of sustained work at RPE 8.5 and 18 working sets per session, your client is carrying meaningful accumulated fatigue even if he feels subjectively good by midweek — which, as discussed, is the deload working correctly rather than a signal to increase intensity. The goal this week is fatigue dissipation and tissue recovery, not fitness maintenance or stimulus. Fitness will be temporarily suppressed and will supercompensate once fatigue clears, which is the precise mechanism the intensification block will exploit from Week 6 onward.

Three rules govern every session this week. First, same exercises as the hypertrophy block, preserving motor patterns without introducing novel fatigue. Second, volume at approximately 50% of recent working sets — 9 sets per session rather than 18. Third, intensity held at RPE 5–6 across all working sets, representing 4–5 reps in reserve at all times. If a set feels easy, that is correct. If the client feels like he could do significantly more, that is also correct, and it should be framed to him as the adaptation mechanism functioning as intended rather than as undertraining.

His shoulder is flagged as cranky on bench press. All horizontal pressing this week uses the low incline dumbbell neutral grip substitution. The reduced load and ROM-friendly position will allow the anterior shoulder structures to recover alongside the rest of the body. Do not reintroduce barbell bench this week regardless of how the shoulder feels by Thursday.

## Strength Tracking Protocol — All Four Resistance Sessions

Run this log on every compound in every resistance session. It generates a fatigue dissipation curve across the week without requiring any maximal effort and gives you clean baseline data for Week 6.

For each compound, record the following at the first working set:

| Exercise | Load Used | Reps Completed | RPE Felt | Bar Speed Feel | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**RPE felt** should be recorded honestly against the prescribed load — if a weight that was RPE 7.5 in week 4 now feels like RPE 5, note that explicitly. That delta is your primary strength marker this week.

**Bar speed feel** should be logged as fast, moderate, or slow. If the gym has a velocity tracking device, log mean concentric velocity numerically. A free app will give rough estimates if no dedicated device is available. Expect velocity at fixed loads to increase across Monday to Friday as fatigue clears. If it doesn't, sleep and nutrition need attention before Week 6 begins.

Do not chase numbers. Do not add reps because the weight feels light. Do not extend any set beyond the prescribed rep target. The tracking is observational, not competitive.

## Monday — Session A: Upper Push

**Warm-up:** 10 minutes. Begin with 5 minutes of light cardio to elevate core temperature — bike or treadmill at an easy pace. Follow with band pull-aparts, wall slides, and two to three progressively loaded warm-up sets on each compound. Warm-up sets do not count toward working sets.

---

**Low Incline Dumbbell Press — Neutral Grip**
*Substituting for barbell bench press due to shoulder irritation*
3 sets × 6 reps — RPE 5–6
Load at approximately 60–65% of the dumbbell or equivalent load used in week 4. The neutral grip reduces internal rotation stress on the anterior shoulder. The low incline — no more than 20–25 degrees — keeps the movement pattern close to flat pressing without the shoulder extension demand of a flat bench. The bottom position should feel comfortable and unstretched. If there is any anterior shoulder discomfort at this position, reduce the range of motion by elevating the dumbbells slightly at the bottom rather than pushing through it. Rest 2 minutes between sets.

**Overhead Press — Barbell or Dumbbell, whichever was used in the hypertrophy block**
3 sets × 6 reps — RPE 5–6
Load at approximately 65% of week 4 working weight. Bar path should be clean and vertical. No excessive lumbar extension to compensate for reduced thoracic mobility. If the shoulder reports any discomfort on the overhead pattern, switch to a landmine press for this week only, which reduces the degree of shoulder elevation and is broadly well-tolerated by irritated anterior shoulders. Rest 2 minutes.

**Cable Fly or Pec Deck — whichever is available**
2 sets × 10 reps — RPE 5
Light load, full range of motion, slow controlled eccentric. This replaces any secondary pressing accessory from the hypertrophy block and keeps mechanical stress off the shoulder while still providing a chest stimulus through the stretch-shortening cycle. Rest 90 seconds.

**Lateral Raises — Dumbbell**
1 set × 12 reps — light
Movement maintenance only. One set is sufficient. Do not add a second set because it feels easy.

**Total working sets: 9**

Session duration should be approximately 40–45 minutes including warm-up. If the client finishes and feels significantly under-stimulated, remind him that the tracking data he just collected is the productive output of the session, not the fatigue generated.

## Wednesday — Mobility Session: 20 Minutes

This is a standalone session, not a warm-up. It should be performed at a genuinely relaxed pace with full attention on quality of movement and breath. Nothing is loaded. Nothing is timed aggressively. The session targets the areas most likely to have accumulated restriction during four weeks of high-volume hypertrophy work — thoracic spine, shoulder girdle, hip flexors, and posterior chain — with additional shoulder-specific work given the flagged irritation.

Complete each drill for the prescribed duration or reps, moving through the sequence without rushing.

---

**Thoracic Spine Foam Roll**
90 seconds. Positioned across a foam roller at mid-back, arms crossed over chest. Slowly extend over the roller, pausing at any stiff segments. Move the roller incrementally up the thoracic spine. Do not roll the lumbar spine. This is the single highest-value mobility drill for someone who has been loading a barbell for four weeks.

**Cat-Cow — Quadruped**
10 slow repetitions. Full spinal flexion to full spinal extension on each rep. Breathe in on extension, out on flexion. This reintroduces segmental spinal movement that gets compressed during heavy loading weeks.

**Thread the Needle — Quadruped Thoracic Rotation**
8 repetitions each side. From a quadruped position, thread one arm under the body and rotate the thoracic spine, following the hand with the eyes. Pause at end range for 2 seconds. This directly addresses thoracic rotation restriction, which contributes to compensatory shoulder stress during pressing.

**90/90 Hip Stretch**
60 seconds each side. Seated on the floor with both legs at 90-degree angles, front and back. Sit tall, breathe into the hip. Progress to a forward fold over the front shin if comfortable. This targets hip external and internal rotation simultaneously and addresses the hip flexor and glute restriction that accumulates during heavy squat and hinge work.

**Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch with Reach**
45 seconds each side. In a half-kneeling position, posteriorly tilt the pelvis, squeeze the glute of the trailing leg, and reach the same-side arm overhead and slightly away from the body. This combines hip flexor lengthening with a lateral thoracic stretch. Given the volume of squatting and deadlifting in the hypertrophy block, hip flexor restriction is almost certain.

**Wall Slide — Shoulder Girdle**
10 repetitions. Standing with back flat against a wall, arms in a goalpost position, slide the arms overhead while maintaining contact between the back of the hands, forearms, and wall. This is directly relevant to the cranky shoulder — it trains scapular upward rotation and posterior shoulder activation in a completely unloaded environment. If the shoulder reports any discomfort during this movement, reduce the range and work only in the pain-free zone.

**Band Pull-Apart or No-Money Drill**
2 × 15 repetitions. Using a light resistance band or no band at all. Pull-aparts target the posterior shoulder and mid-traps, which are chronically under-recovered in pressing-dominant programmes. The no-money drill — starting with elbows at 90 degrees and externally rotating — specifically targets the infraspinatus and teres minor, which are relevant to anterior shoulder health.

**Doorframe or Rack Pec Stretch — Modified**
30 seconds each side. Using a rack upright rather than a doorframe for better control. Position the arm at 90 degrees of abduction — not higher — and gently lean into the stretch. Given the shoulder irritation, do not force this stretch and do not position the arm above shoulder height. A mild pull in the pec is appropriate. Any anterior shoulder pain means stopping immediately.

**Child's Pose with Lat Reach**
60 seconds. From child's pose, walk the hands to one side to bias the lat and thoracic side bend. 30 seconds each side. The lats are heavily loaded during rowing and pulling work and their restriction directly affects shoulder positioning during pressing.

**Diaphragmatic Breathing — Supine**
2 minutes. Lying on the back, knees bent, one hand on the chest and one on the belly. Breathe into the belly, allowing the diaphragm to descend. Exhale fully. This is not filler — diaphragmatic breathing directly downregulates the sympathetic nervous system and supports the recovery process. For an advanced client who has been training at high intensity for four weeks, deliberate parasympathetic activation has measurable recovery value.

**Total session time: approximately 18–22 minutes**

## Saturday — Zone 2 Cardio: 30 Minutes

**Modality:** Cycling or incline treadmill walk — adjust based on client preference and equipment availability. Rowing is excluded this week given the shoulder. Running is appropriate if the client has a conditioning base, but given four weeks of pure hypertrophy work, cycling or walking is the lower-risk default.

**Intensity:** Heart rate 116–136 bpm, based on estimated max HR of 194 bpm for a 26-year-old. If the client has a measured max HR, recalculate the band as 60–70% of that figure. The talk test is a reliable field check — he should be able to hold a full conversation without any breathlessness. If he cannot, the intensity is too high.

**Structure:** No warm-up or cool-down protocol required beyond the first and last few minutes of the session naturally sitting below the Zone 2 band. 30 minutes of continuous steady-state work. No intervals, no surges, no pushing the upper end of the HR band. This is aerobic system maintenance, not a cardiovascular training stimulus.

**Purpose:** Four weeks of high-volume hypertrophy work with no dedicated aerobic work will have modestly reduced mitochondrial density and cardiac output efficiency. Two Zone 2 sessions this week maintain the aerobic base without generating any fatigue that competes with the recovery process. Zone 2 work at this intensity also actively supports recovery by increasing blood flow to recovering tissues and enhancing lactate clearance.

## Nutrition This Week

Maintain caloric intake at the same absolute level as the hypertrophy block. Do not reduce calories in response to the reduced training volume. The body is in an active repair and consolidation phase and requires adequate energy availability to complete that process. Reducing calories during a deload is a common mistake that blunts the recovery effect and compromises the supercompensation response going into Week 6.

Protein remains at a minimum of 1.8–2.2g per kilogram of bodyweight. Carbohydrates should be maintained — glycogen replenishment supports recovery and there is no metabolic rationale for reducing carbohydrate intake during a single-week deload. If the client is in a caloric surplus, maintain it. If in a deficit, bring calories to maintenance for this week specifically.

Hydration deserves particular attention this week. Connective tissue recovery — relevant given the shoulder — is directly supported by adequate hydration. Target a minimum of 35ml per kilogram of bodyweight per day.

## Sleep and Recovery

Target 8 hours per night with consistent sleep and wake times across the week. Growth hormone secretion during slow-wave sleep is a primary driver of the tissue repair that makes the deload productive. This is the week to be deliberate about sleep quality, not just duration — dark room, cool temperature, no screens in the 30 minutes before bed.

Alcohol should be minimised or eliminated this week. It directly impairs slow-wave sleep architecture and inhibits muscle protein synthesis, both of which undermine the recovery process.

If the client uses any recovery modalities — contrast showers, sauna, soft tissue work — this is an appropriate week to use them. A sports massage midweek, if accessible, would be particularly well-timed given the accumulated tissue stress from the hypertrophy block.

## End-of-Week Assessment

By Friday evening you should have four sessions of tracking data. Review the RPE and velocity logs and ask three questions before finalising the Week 6 programme.

First, did RPE at fixed loads drop across the week? A load that was RPE 7.5 in week 4 should feel like RPE 5–5.5 by Friday. If it does, the deload has worked and Week 6 can begin at full intensity. If it hasn't moved, consider one additional lighter day before ramping up.

Second, how is the shoulder? It should feel meaningfully better than it did at the end of week 4. If it does, the bench substitution decision for Week 6 can be revisited carefully. If it is still irritated, the neutral grip incline press stays in the programme and a physio referral is worth raising with the client.

Third, how is the client's motivation and psychological state? An advanced client who is genuinely bored and hungry to train hard by Friday is in the ideal state to begin an intensification block. That is the target outcome of this week.
